extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; literate early-18th-century urban middle/upper classes interested in manners, morals, and social satire
extracted.subtask_description: Speculative/satirical periodical essays addressing manners, conduct, and social custom, written for an educated urban readership and exemplifying moral criticism with wit and anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matchmaking for profit (Sempronia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sempronia 'supports herself in an affluent Condition, by contracting Friendship with rich young Widows and Maids of plentiful Fortunes at their own Disposal, and bestowing her Friends upon worthless indigent Fellows; on the other Side, she ensnares inconsiderate and rash Youths of great Estates into the Arms of vitious Women.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed depiction of the arts she uses: being accomplished at impertinent visits, knowing servants and dependants, procuring outfits or adding 'virtues' (good humour, sobriety) to a worthless man, and hastening matches by importunities and devices. Anti-pattern: raising profit by abuses is judged worse than theft because it makes lives permanently unhappy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental sacrifice of talent for fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: A Parent who forces a Child of a liberal and ingenious Spirit into the Arms of a Clown or a Blockhead 'obliges her to a Crime too odious for a Name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong moral condemnation: forcing accomplished children into unequal marriages is unnatural and yields lasting misery. The essay foregrounds the duty to value sense and merit over mere wealth and warns against parents preferring social conspicuousness or fortune over their children's happiness and intellectual gifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Societal preference for wealth over happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that many mothers 'had rather see their Children miserable in great Wealth, than the happiest of the Race of Mankind in a less conspicuous State of Life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of social values that prize outward fortune above private happiness; used to explain why matches like Favilla's occur and why Sempronia prospers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Containment of anger as moral discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: To contain the Spirit of Anger is 'the worthiest Discipline we can put our selves to' and should be 'the Study of every Man, for his own Quiet and Peace.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that quick sensibility must be subordinated to reason; examples of impertinent passionate behaviour (insulting servants, throwing plates, public humiliations) illustrate harms. Cites great examples of self-mastery (Lord Somers) and contrasts passionate overflow with absurd theatrical rage. Normative: mastery of anger elevates a person and spares family/friends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of angry temperaments and their faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification: (a) passionate Men—violent, transient outbursts that do lasting social harm; (b) peevish Fellows—habitual sourness, censoriousness and incapacity for delight; (c) Snarlers—ironic, hectoring, especially toward inferiors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type is described with typical behaviours (e.g., passionate men assemble allusions to wound, peevish men use 'Pish' and 'Pshaw' and resist pleasure, snarler uses irony to servants). Practical guidance: these humours should not be indulged; society should refuse toleration of habitual ill manners except by those who must be waited on for bread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of toleration for habitual peculiarities
rubrics_metrics.description: No Man ought to be tolerated in an habitual Humour, Whim, or Particularity of Behaviour, by any who do not wait upon him for Bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm for polite company: habitual eccentric or offensive behaviour is not grounds for indulgence; tolerance is limited by dependency relationships. This is given as a standard for when social patience is and is not owed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of resignation and patience about trifles
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice, illustrated by the book-lending anecdote: learn resignation to small losses and 'be patient; the Book is lost, but do not you for that Reason lose your self.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical moral: avoid letting trifles provoke anger; cultivate forbearance to prevent unnecessary misery. The anecdote shows how passion prevents hearing reason and escalates disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and danger of spies/informers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers use 'other People's Eyes and Ears' but must do it 'in such a manner, that it may not bear too hard on the Person whose Life and Conversation are enquired into.' A spy 'naturally inflames every Word and Circumstance, aggravates what is faulty, perverts what is good, and misrepresents what is indifferent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary standard for employing intelligence: spies are untrustworthy, prone to exaggeration and private malice, and their reports will often be more flattering to their patron than true. Example: an Italian anecdote of a spy who reports insults until his patron (a Cardinal) expels him. Recommendation: exercise prudence and restraint when using clandestine information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid obsessive curiosity about reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Great and heroic minds show disregard for unmerited reproaches and do not 'inquiring after them' or 'the poor Revenge of resenting them.' In contrast, a man 'inquisitive after every thing which is spoken ill of him, passes his Time but very indifferently.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm: do not torment yourself by seeking or obsessing over every whisper; such curiosity wounds and often worsens one's condition by provoking further exposure. The essay concludes with Clarendon's character of a great man undone by impertinent curiosity about private remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of polite company: 'Infirmary' rules for behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules from a society's week of proceedings: offences leading to removal to the Infirmary include swearing at a servant, long fits of dulness or boobyish behaviour (contempt of company), insolent replies and quarrels at table, continual complaint about dishes or refusal to laugh, making offensive puns to a neighbour with antipathy, noisy disputants who raise voice and thump the table, and voluntarily shutting oneself up in an unsociable temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model of enforcement: a President moderates, orders offenders conveyed to an infirmary, applies suitable remedies (confinement, diet of water-gruel, denial of writing implements until reflection, or being put aside as a 'Weather-glass'). The guidance shows concrete sanctions for breaches of civility and a practical institutional approach to cultivating agreeable conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in the Supreme Being as a moral resource
rubrics_metrics.description: The person 'who has a firm trust on the Supreme Being is Powerful in his Power, Wise by his Wisdom, Happy by his Happiness.' Such trust 'contributes very much to the getting clear of any Affliction, or to the bearing it manfully.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral/spiritual criterion: reliance on divine providence produces patience, hope, cheerfulness, fortitude in adversity, and comfort at the hour of death. The essay adduces historical and pastoral imagery (translation of the 23rd Psalm) to recommend trust as a practical virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial ethics for publishing correspondents' papers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectator's editor explains he at first altered contributors' papers to fit his style, but upon review found some so 'extremely natural and peculiarly good' that 'I think I should not only wrong them, but deprive the World of a considerable Satisfaction, should I any longer delay the making them publick' and therefore will print some 'entire, and without any Alteration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for handling submissions: when a correspondent's paper is natural and would be harmed by alteration, publish it intact. Also prescribes editorial humility—an author should 'take all Methods to humble himself in the Opinion he has of his own Performances' and not exclude other 'Spectators.'
